location: Book 9, paragraph 0 — Opening — Odysseus begins his tale
Candidate A:
And Ulysses answered, “King Alcinous, it is a good thing to hear a bard
with such a divine voice as this man has. There is nothing better or
more delightful than when a whole people make merry together, with the
guests sitting orderly to listen, while the table is loaded with bread
and meats, and the cup-bearer draws wine and fills his cup for every
man. This is indeed as fair a sight as a man can see. Now, however,
since you are inclined to ask the story of my sorrows, and rekindle my
own sad memories in respect of them, I do not know how to begin, nor
yet how to continue and conclude my tale, for the hand of heaven has
been laid heavily upon me.
Candidate B: And Odysseus answered, "King Alcinous, it is a wonderful thing to hear a singer with such a divine voice as this man has. There is nothing better or more delightful than when a whole people celebrate together, with the guests sitting in order to listen, while the table is loaded with bread and meat, and the cup-bearer draws wine and fills each man's cup. This is truly as beautiful a sight as anyone can see. Now, however, since you want to hear the story of my sorrows, and rekindle my own sad memories of them, I don't know how to begin, or how to continue and end my tale, for the hand of heaven has weighed heavily upon me.
Candidate C: Odysseus answered, “King Alcinous, it's a fine thing to listen to a singer with a voice as god-given as this one has. There is nothing better or more pleasant than when a whole people feast together in good order, the guests seated and listening while the tables are loaded with bread and meat, and the steward draws wine and fills every man's cup. That is as beautiful a sight as anyone could see. But now, since you want to hear the story of my sufferings, and so stir up my grief all over again, I hardly know where to begin, or how to go on and bring the tale to its end, for the gods have laid a heavy hand on me.

location: Book 9, paragraph 12 — Inside the cave — dramatic irony, the men's warning ignored
Candidate A: "We soon reached his cave, but he was out shepherding, so we went inside and looked at everything we could see. His cheese-racks were loaded with cheeses, and he had more lambs and kids than his pens could hold. They were kept in separate flocks; first there were the yearlings, then the older of the younger lambs and lastly the very young ones all kept apart from one another; as for his dairy, all the vessels, bowls, and milk pails into which he milked, were swimming with whey. When they saw all this, my men begged me to let them first steal some cheeses, and make off with them to the ship; they would then return, drive down the lambs and kids, put them on board and sail away with them. It would have been much better if we had done so but I would not listen to them, for I wanted to see the owner himself, in the hope that he might give me a gift. When, however, we saw him my poor men found him terrible to deal with.

location: Book 9, paragraph 18 — First killing — the horror of the feast
Candidate A:
“The cruel wretch vouchsafed me not one word of answer, but with a
sudden clutch he gripped up two of my men at once and dashed them down
upon the ground as though they had been puppies. Their brains were shed
upon the ground, and the earth was wet with their blood. Then he tore
them limb from limb and supped upon them. He gobbled them up like a
lion in the wilderness, flesh, bones, marrow, and entrails, without
leaving anything uneaten. As for us, we wept and lifted up our hands to
heaven on seeing such a horrid sight, for we did not know what else to
do; but when the Cyclops had filled his huge paunch, and had washed
down his meal of human flesh with a drink of neat milk, he stretched
himself full length upon the ground among his sheep, and went to sleep.
I was at first inclined to seize my sword, draw it, and drive it into
his vitals, but I reflected that if I did we should all certainly be
lost, for we should never be able to shift the stone which the monster
had put in front of the door. So we stayed sobbing and sighing where we
were till morning came.

location: Book 9, paragraph 25 — The blinding of the Cyclops
Candidate A: “As he spoke he reeled and fell backward, sprawled on the ground, and a deep sleep took hold of him. His head lolled back over his great neck. Soon he began to retch, bringing up wine and gobbets of human flesh together, for he was very drunk. Then I thrust the stake deep into the embers to heat it, and spoke to my men to keep their courage up, in case any of them lost heart. When the wood, green as it was, was just about to catch fire and glow, I drew it from the flames, and my men gathered round me, for some god had filled their hearts with courage. We drove the sharpened point into the monster's eye, and I leaned my whole weight on it and twisted it round and round, the way a man bores a hole in a ship's timber with an auger, which two men can keep turning as long as they like with a wheel and strap. So we turned the red-hot stake in his eye, until the blood boiled up around it, and the steam from the scorching eyeball singed his brow and lashes, and the roots of the eye crackled in the fire. As a blacksmith plunges a red-hot axe or adze into cold water to temper it—for that is what gives strength to iron—and it hisses loudly as he does, so his eye hissed around the olive stake. He gave a terrible scream, and the cave rang with it. We ran back in terror, but he wrenched the stake, dripping with blood, out of his eye and hurled it from him, howling in a frenzy of pain, and calling out to the other Cyclopes who lived scattered on the windswept heights nearby. They heard him and came from every side, gathering round the cave to ask what was wrong with him.

location: Book 9, paragraph 32 — Polyphemus talks to the ram
Candidate A: "'My good ram, what is it that makes you the last to leave my cave this morning? You are not used to letting the ewes go before you, but lead the flock at a run whether to flowery meadow or bubbling fountain, and are the first to come home again at night; but now you lag last of all. Is it because you know your master has lost his eye, and are sorry because that wicked Nobody and his horrible crew got him down in his drink and blinded him? But I will have his life yet. If you could understand and talk, you would tell me where the wretch is hiding, and I would dash his brains upon the ground until they flew all over the cave. location: Book 9, paragraph 38 — Polyphemus recognizes the prophecy
Candidate A:
“On this he groaned, and cried out, ‘Alas, alas, then the old prophecy
about me is coming true. There was a prophet here, at one time, a man
both brave and of great stature, Telemus son of Eurymus, who was an
excellent seer, and did all the prophesying for the Cyclopes till he
grew old; he told me that all this would happen to me some day, and
said I should lose my sight by the hand of Ulysses. I have been all
